title: Leading Those Who Rationalize Poor Performance
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece addresses the phenomenon of 'defensive attribution', the near-universal tendency of poor performers to blame external factors for their own results, and argues leaders shouldn't waste effort trying to get people to fully own their rationalizations. Instead, the piece recommends shifting the conversation entirely toward a concrete plan of specific actions the person will take differently going forward. This works, the author argues, because even people highly inclined toward defensive attribution will still agree to try something new. The piece cites Martin Luther King Jr.'s 'keep moving' quote.
points: 'Defensive attribution', blaming external factors for poor performance, is described as a near-universal human tendency, not a character flaw.
Rather than pushing people to 'own' their poor performance, the piece recommends redirecting toward specific planned actions going forward.
Even people highly resistant to accepting blame for past results will typically still agree to commit to a concrete plan of new actions.
Requiring a precise plan of action, rather than litigating root causes, reduces defensiveness.
quotes: Poor performers are notorious for explaining why their inferior results have little to do with them.

By attributing poor results to factors outside of their control, people minimize their accountability for past, present, and future outcomes. This is a neat trick. Unfortunately, however, they don’t get any better.
The key is not for leaders to get people to “own” their poor performance and to stare it down. Rather, the magic is in asking what they are going do differently to achieve a better result.
Good leaders ask poor performers to be specific. They demand a precise plan of action that will create change.
By pushing people to decide what they will do differently, leaders confront poorly performing team members with the leadership they so desperately need.
